It carries all their iniquities away with it. In 1530, translating the Bible into English, William Tyndale coined the word scapegoat; in French, one says bouc émissaire.
Les Grecs aussi avaient leurs boucs émis: The Greeks had their scapegoats too, human ones. In times of famine, drought or plague, one or two poor people, slaves or criminals were driven out to save the city. In Abdera, a poor man was well fed, led around the walls, then driven out with stones. In Massalia, one was fed for a year before being cast out to stop an epidemic.
Le bouc émissaire porte les fautes de to: The scapegoat bears everyone's sins: an ancient rite turned reflex, naming a culprit when misfortune strikes.
La peste noire atteint l'Europe en 1347: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 and within a few years killed 30 to 60 percent of Europeans, depending on the estimate. No one knew its cause. From 1348 to 1351, a rumour spread: Jews were said to be poisoning the wells. Some, under torture, ended up "confessing". Massacres followed one another, from Toulon in April 1348 to Basel, Erfurt, Mainz, Frankfurt or Zurich; some 510 Jewish communities were destroyed.
Le 14 février 1349, à Strasbourg, enviro: On 14 February 1349, in Strasbourg, about 2,000 Jews were burned alive, although the plague had not yet reached the city. Pope Clement VI had nevertheless issued two bulls, on 6 July and 26 September 1348: Jews are dying of the plague too, and it strikes regions where there are none. The argument was unanswerable; the rumour was stronger. In Poland, King Casimir III welcomed the refugees.
1348-1351 : face à une cause inconnue, l: 1348-1351: faced with an unknown cause, rumour names a culprit, and even an unanswerable argument does not stop it.
Des années 1400 aux années 1770, l'Europ: From the 1400s to the 1770s, Europe tried witches. The Hammer of Witches, by the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer, appeared in Speyer in 1486; it claims that women yield more easily to the devil and served as a manual for secular courts. The trials peaked from 1560 to 1630 and killed 40,000 to 60,000 people; about 80 percent of those convicted were women.
Des historiens comme Wolfgang Behringer: Historians such as Wolfgang Behringer or Emily Oster note that trials increased as the climate cooled: lost harvests, wars, diseases, and witches as culprits. The explanation is judged too simple, but it recalls the plague. As early as 1563, the physician Johann Weyer argued that accused women who confessed were sick, melancholic, not allies of the devil.
Les sorcières ont servi de boucs émissai: Witches served as scapegoats for Europe's misfortunes: 40,000 to 60,000 dead.
Les idoles des deux Bacon: The idols of the two Bacons
En 1267, Roger Bacon dénonce quatre caus: In 1267, Roger Bacon denounced four causes of error; in 1620, Francis Bacon listed the idols that distort the mind.
Les idoles des deux Bacon, dans le temps: The idols of the two Bacons, in time
Roger Bacon, Opus majus, 1267 : se fier: Roger Bacon, Opus Majus, 1267: relying on weak authority, custom, the ignorance of the crowd, and ignorance hidden behind a show of knowledge.
Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, 1620 : les: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, 1620: the idols of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre.

« Où sont les portraits de ceux qui se s: "Where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?": counting only the survivors misleads.
Les idoles de Bacon ne sont pas des stat: Bacon's idols are not statues: they are false images in the mind, from the Latin idola.
En 1267, à la demande du pape Clément IV: In 1267, at the request of Pope Clement IV, the scholar Roger Bacon sent him his Opus Majus, the "Greater Work". The first of its seven parts deals with the obstacles to wisdom and truth. He sorts four causes of error: relying on weak or unreliable authority, following custom, sharing the ignorance of the crowd, and hiding one's own ignorance behind a show of knowledge.
Le reste de l'ouvrage fait la part belle: The rest of the work gives pride of place to observation. The fifth part, on optics, draws on the Arab scholars al-Kindi and Alhazen; the sixth is devoted to "experimental science". There is also alchemy and a taste for magic: Bacon was a man of his time, but he had seen that authority and habit lead the mind astray.
Roger Bacon, 1267 : l'autorité, la coutu: Roger Bacon, 1267: authority, custom, the opinion of the crowd and false knowledge are the four sources of error.
En 1620, le philosophe anglais Francis B: In 1620, the English philosopher Francis Bacon published, in Latin, the Novum Organum, the second part of a grand project to renew the sciences, the Instauratio Magna. On the frontispiece, a galleon sails past the Pillars of Hercules. But before proposing his method, Bacon lists the "idols", the false images that clutter the mind.
Les idoles de la tribu tiennent à la nat: The idols of the tribe are rooted in human nature: we see more order in nature than there is. Those of the cave come from each individual, from temperament and upbringing: each has his own cave, which scatters and discolours the light. Those of the marketplace arise from misunderstood words. Those of the theatre, finally, come from philosophical systems accepted without examination, like those of Aristotle or Plato.
Tribu, caverne, place publique, théâtre: Tribe, cave, marketplace, theatre: the species, the individual, words and doctrines distort our judgement.
Dans l'aphorisme 46, Bacon décrit avec t: In aphorism 46, Bacon described three centuries ahead what would be called confirmation bias: once it has adopted an opinion, the human understanding draws everything else to support and agree with it. It keeps the favourable cases, and neglects or sets aside those that contradict it.
Il raconte qu'on montra à un homme, dans: He tells how a man was shown, in a temple, the pictures offered by those who had made a vow and escaped shipwreck, to make him acknowledge the power of the gods. He asked: "But where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?" According to ancient sources, the retort belongs to Diagoras, in Cicero, or to Diogenes the Cynic.
Ne compter que les rescapés, c'est se tr: Counting only the survivors is a sure way to be wrong: one must also look for the drowned.
À Paris et à Londres, en 1720, les actio: In Paris and London, in 1720, Mississippi and South Sea shares soared then collapsed: everyone was counting on selling for more.
1720, l'année des bulles, dans le temps: 1720, the year of bubbles, in time
À Paris, l'action de la Compagnie du Mis: In Paris, John Law's Mississippi Company share went from 500 to 10,000 livres, then collapsed in 1720.
À Londres, l'action de la Compagnie des: In London, the South Sea Company share rose from £128 in January 1720 to £1,000 in August, and fell back to £150 by the end of September.
Le mot « bulle » vient de cet épisode :: The word "bubble" comes from this episode: prices inflated with nothing but air.
Théorie du plus grand imbécile : on achè: Greater fool theory: people buy too dear, counting on selling dearer still. The bubble bursts when there are no more buyers.
La phrase de Newton sur « la folie des g: Newton's line about "the madness of people" is known only at second hand, and no one knows how much he really lost.
À Paris, l'économiste écossais John Law: In Paris, the Scottish economist John Law founded in 1717 a company that received all of Louisiana and a monopoly on its trade: the future Mississippi Company. Its shares, issued at 500 livres, stayed at that price until mid-1719. Then the fever rose: the price reached 10,000 livres. People fought over them in the open air, on the rue Quincampoix. In February 1720, the company even bought the Banque Royale.
Pour suivre la demande d'actions, il fau: To keep up with the demand for shares, ever more bank notes were needed, and inflation reached 23 percent a month in January 1720. Then the bubble burst: 2,000 livres in September 1720, 1,000 in December. By the end of the year, the Regent, Philippe d'Orléans, had dismissed Law, who fled to Brussels, then to Venice.
Paris, 1719-1720 : de 500 à 10 000 livre: Paris, 1719-1720: from 500 to 10,000 livres, then 1,000. The rise drew buyers, and the buyers made the rise.
À Londres, la même année, l'action de la: In London, the same year, the South Sea Company share went from about £128 in January 1720 to £550 at the end of May, then £1,000 in early August. In the fever, many dubious companies sprang up, already called "bubbles". The most famous supposedly raised funds "for carrying out an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is"; it is probably a legend.
Fin septembre, l'action ne vaut plus que: By the end of September, the share was worth only £150, and about £100 by the end of the year. The 33 directors were removed and lost on average 82 percent of their wealth. Isaac Newton held nearly £22,000 of stock in 1722; he is said to have lost up to £20,000 and to have said he "could not calculate the madness of people", but these words are known only at second hand.
Londres, 1720 : 128 £, 1 000 £, puis 150: London, 1720: £128, £1,000, then £150. A bubble rises because people buy, and bursts when they stop buying.
Pourquoi acheter une action manifestemen: Why buy a share that is plainly too dear? Because you count on selling it dearer still to someone else: that is the greater fool theory. As long as new buyers arrive, drawn by the first ones' gains and the fear of missing out, the price rises. But, as the economist Burton Malkiel puts it, eventually one runs out of greater fools.
L'économiste Charles Kindleberger, auteu: The economist Charles Kindleberger, author in 1978 of a history of financial crises, described bubbles in five phases: a shock that opens new opportunities for profit, the boom, euphoria, distress when prices level off, then revulsion when everyone sells. Every time, people tell themselves that "this time is different". The word bubble itself comes from the South Sea affair: prices inflated with nothing but air.
Une bulle vit de l'espoir de revendre pl: A bubble lives on the hope of selling for more: it bursts when there is no greater fool left.
De Charles Mackay, en 1841, à Allport et: From Charles Mackay, in 1841, to Allport and Postman, in 1947: how a false idea runs faster than the true one.
En 1785, Condorcet calcule quand une maj: In 1785, Condorcet calculated when a majority is right; in 1907, Galton saw a crowd guess the weight of an ox. Provided everyone thinks alone.
La sagesse des foules, dans le temps: The wisdom of crowds, in time
Théorème du jury de Condorcet, 1785 : si: Condorcet's jury theorem, 1785: if each voter has more than an even chance of being right and votes independently, the more voters there are, the likelier the majority is to be right.
Galton, 1907 : à Plymouth, l'estimation: Galton, 1907: at Plymouth, the median estimate of 787 tickets, 1,207 pounds, came within 9 pounds of the ox's real weight, 1,198.
Surowiecki, 2004 : une foule est sage si: Surowiecki, 2004: a crowd is wise if opinions are diverse, independent, decentralised and well aggregated.
Zurich, 2011 : montrer aux gens les esti: Zurich, 2011: showing people the others' estimates reduces diversity without making the crowd more accurate.
Si chacun a moins d'une chance sur deux: If each has less than an even chance of being right, adding voters makes things worse: the best jury is then a single voter.
Bien avant les sondages, Aristote notait: Long before opinion polls, Aristotle noted in his Politics that the many may be better, not individually but collectively, like a dinner to which each contributes. In 1785, Condorcet gave a mathematical version of it in his Essay on the Application of Analysis to the Probability of Majority Decisions.
C'est le théorème du jury : si chaque vo: This is the jury theorem: if each voter has a probability p, greater than 1/2, of voting correctly, independently of the others, then the more voters there are, the likelier the majority is to be right, approaching certainty. With three voters at p = 0.8, the majority is right with a probability of 0.896. But if p is below 1/2, each extra voter makes things worse.
Condorcet, 1785 : une majorité de votant: Condorcet, 1785: a majority of independent voters, each a little better than chance, is very often right.
À une foire aux bestiaux de Plymouth, en: At a livestock fair in Plymouth, in 1906, about 800 visitors placed bets on the weight of an ox once slaughtered and dressed. The statistician Francis Galton collected the 787 legible tickets.
En 1907, il publie le résultat dans la r: In 1907, he published the result in the journal Nature, under the title Vox Populi. The median estimate, 1,207 pounds, was only 9 pounds off the real weight, 1,198: under 1 percent. The mean of the tickets, published later, came to 1,197. Taken together, the crowd had got it right.
Galton, 1907 : la médiane de 787 estimat: Galton, 1907: the median of 787 estimates came within 1 percent of the ox's true weight.
Quand la foule perd sa sagesse: When the crowd loses its wisdom
En 2004, James Surowiecki popularise l'i: In 2004, James Surowiecki popularised the idea in The Wisdom of Crowds. A crowd is wise under four conditions: diversity of opinion, independence, decentralisation, and a good way to aggregate views. It fails through homogeneity, centralisation, division, imitation or emotionality.
En 2011, à l'École polytechnique fédéral: In 2011, at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich, researchers had 144 students estimate six quantities, such as the population density of Switzerland. When shown the others' answers, their estimates converged without becoming more accurate, and their confidence rose. Social influence destroys the diversity that made the crowd wise.
Une foule n'est sage que si chacun pense: A crowd is wise only if each person thinks alone: imitation makes it confident, not more accurate.
En 1932, Frederic Bartlett montre que se: In 1932, Frederic Bartlett showed that remembering is rebuilding; in 1974, Elizabeth Loftus changed a memory with a single verb.
En 1943, Abraham Wald blinde les avions: In 1943, Abraham Wald armoured planes where no hits could be seen; in 1973, Tversky and Kahneman showed that we judge frequency by what comes to mind.
En 1951, Solomon Asch montre qu'on cède: In 1951, Solomon Asch showed that people yield to a unanimous group that is wrong; in 1972, Irving Janis named groupthink.
En 1948, Skinner rend des pigeons supers: In 1948, Skinner made pigeons superstitious; in 1956, Festinger observed believers whose prophecy failed.
En 1960, Peter Wason invente le jeu 2-4-: In 1960, Peter Wason invented the 2-4-6 game, then in 1966 his four cards: we look for what proves us right and ignore the rest.
Berkeley, 1973 : des chiffres qui s'inve: Berkeley, 1973: figures that reverse when grouped; then regression to the mean and false positives.
En 1974, Tversky et Kahneman font tourne: In 1974, Tversky and Kahneman spun a rigged wheel: a first number, however absurd, pulls our estimates.
En 1979, Kahneman et Tversky publient la: In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky published prospect theory: losing hurts more than winning pleases. Then sunk costs and nudges.
En 1986, Harry Frankfurt distingue le me: In 1986, Harry Frankfurt distinguished the liar from the bullshitter; in 2013, Alberto Brandolini measured what it costs to refute nonsense.
Frankfurt, 1986 : le menteur connaît la: Frankfurt, 1986: the liar knows the truth and hides it; the bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true.
D'où sa formule : le baratin est un plus: Hence his formula: bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are.
Pennycook, 2015 : des phrases fabriquées: Pennycook, 2015: sentences randomly built from buzzwords are rated fairly profound, 2.6 out of 5 on average.
Loi de Brandolini, 2013 : réfuter une ân: Brandolini's law, 2013: refuting nonsense takes ten times more energy than producing it.
Une phrase creuse peut être grammaticale: A hollow sentence can be grammatically perfect: "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty" means nothing.
En 1986, le philosophe Harry Frankfurt p: In 1986, the philosopher Harry Frankfurt published in the journal Raritan an essay with an unacademic title, On Bullshit. He starts from a notion of the philosopher Max Black, humbug, more polite but close.
Sa distinction est restée célèbre : le m: His distinction became famous: the liar cares about the truth, since he tries to hide it. The bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true or false; only the effect counts. Hence his conclusion: bullshit is a greater enemy of the truth than lies are. Republished as a small book in 2005, the essay spent 27 weeks on the New York Times best-seller list.
Le menteur cache la vérité ; le baratine: The liar hides the truth; the bullshitter ignores it. Frankfurt, 1986: the second is the more dangerous.
En 2015, Gordon Pennycook et quatre coll: In 2015, Gordon Pennycook and four colleagues built meaningless sentences out of buzzwords, using two online generators, one of which drew on the tweets of the author Deepak Chopra. Example: "Hidden meaning transforms unparalleled abstract beauty." The grammar is perfect; the meaning, absent.
Les participants notent la profondeur de: Participants rated the profundity of each sentence from 1 to 5. Average: 2.6, between "somewhat" and "fairly" profound. Those who saw the most profundity did worse on reflective-thinking tests and made more ontological confusions. In a second study, real vague tweets by Chopra received ratings similar to those of the random sentences.
Une phrase qui sonne profond n'est pas p: A sentence that sounds profound is not profound: ask what exactly it claims.
En janvier 2013, le programmeur italien: In January 2013, the Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini formulated his law: the amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it. He had just read Daniel Kahneman's book on the two systems of thought, then watched a TV debate with Silvio Berlusconi and Marco Travaglio.
L'idée est ancienne. En 1710, Jonathan S: The idea is old. In 1710, Jonathan Swift wrote that falsehood flies, and truth comes limping after it. In 1845, Frédéric Bastiat noted in his Economic Sophisms that a half-truth can be stated in a few words, but refuting it requires long and dry dissertations. An order of magnitude is a factor of ten.
Produire du baratin coûte peu, le démont: Producing bullshit costs little, taking it apart costs ten times more: hence the point of not passing it on.
En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger measured the gap between what we know and what we think we know.
Pré-mortem de Gary Klein en 2007, lectur: Gary Klein's pre-mortem in 2007, lateral reading in 2017, forecasts in probabilities: today's tools against our biases.
